The Centre for Peace and Development, Veritas University, Abuja, has called on the Federal Government to place human rights, civilian protection and national sovereignty at the centre of Nigeria’s counter-terrorism operations, warning against foreign military intervention without clear legal safeguards. The centre also urged Nigeria and the United States to strengthen their security partnership through intelligence sharing, technical assistance and institutional capacity-building, rather than relying largely on military operations to tackle terrorism. The recommendations were contained in a communiqué issued at the end of a roundtable and mini-conference organised by CEPAD in collaboration with the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, West Africa, at Veritas University, Abuja. The communiqué was released on Monday. The conference, themed, ‘Counter-terrorism in Nigeria and United States Military Intervention: Rethinking the Responsibility to Protect’, brought together academics, researchers, security practitioners and students to examine Nigeria’s security challenges and the implications of possible United States military engagement. According to the communiqué, terrorism remains a major threat to Nigeria’s national security, human security, social cohesion and sustainable development, requiring responses beyond military action. It stated that counter-terrorism strategies must address the political, socioeconomic, ideological and institutional conditions sustaining violent extremism. The conference noted that although United States security assistance had strengthened Nigeria’s counter-terrorism capacity through intelligence, training, surveillance and logistics, it had not decisively defeated insurgent groups, including Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province. It also identified human rights violations, weak intelligence, corruption and governance deficits as factors undermining the effectiveness of counter-terrorism operations. On the Responsibility to Protect framework, the participants warned against interpreting it as an unrestricted justification for unilateral military intervention. Its application must remain consistent with the principles and procedures of international law and the United Nations Charter.” It further stressed that Nigeria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity must be respected in all forms of international security engagement, while recognising the government’s responsibility to protect citizens against terrorism and mass atrocities. The conference called for stronger mechanisms to protect religious minorities, vulnerable communities and places of worship, warning that counter-terrorism policies must avoid religious profiling, discrimination and the stigmatisation of particular religious groups. On civilian protection, the participants recommended independent monitoring of military operations, credible investigations into allegations of civilian casualties and accountability procedures for human rights violations. They also called for greater community participation in intelligence gathering, early warning and the prevention of violent extremism. Presenting a paper on Nigeria-US counter-terrorism cooperation, a lecturer in the Departments of Political Science and Diplomacy, and Peace and Conflict Studies at Veritas University, Emmanuella Onota, argued that the partnership should be assessed not only by its military achievements but also by its contribution to civilian protection. She identified security coordination gaps, civilian casualties, weak accountability and inadequate community participation as challenges undermining security operations. Onota also emphasised the importance of community knowledge and participation in preventing violent extremism, cautioning against arming local communities without effective oversight or treating civil society organisations merely as intelligence sources. Similarly, Dr Roberts Anya Nkata, in his presentation on civilian protection and US military engagement in Nigeria, argued that military assistance alone could not guarantee effective counter-terrorism or civilian protection. Nkata proposed what he described as “protection-conditioned security assistance”, linking military support to accountability, lawful operations, civilian protection and institutional learning. He recommended stronger monitoring of US security assistance, improved target verification, credible investigations of civilian harm and joint assessments of security operations by Nigeria and the United States. Also speaking, Rev. Fr. Dr Isaac Vasumu Augustine, who examined religious freedom and counter-terrorism, identified terrorism, religious intolerance, weak governance, poverty and socioeconomic exclusion as interconnected drivers of insecurity. He said the activities of Boko Haram, ISWAP and other violent groups had contributed to killings, displacement, abductions and violations of religious freedom. Augustine called for stronger intelligence cooperation, human rights accountability, interreligious dialogue, good governance and socioeconomic development to address the underlying causes of insecurity. In his presentation on the international legal basis of US military engagement in Nigeria, Dr Chukwudi Victor Odoeme examined the tension between national sovereignty and international counter-terrorism obligations. He argued that Nigeria’s consent to joint military operations could provide a potential legal justification for US military engagement, but noted that the absence of publicly available details concerning such consent left aspects of the intervention’s legality unresolved. Odoeme stressed that any foreign military intervention must comply with the principles of valid state consent, necessity, proportionality and international law. The communiqué further recommended strengthening Nigeria’s security institutions, institutionalising the participation of religious leaders and faith-based organisations in peacebuilding, and deepening regional cooperation through the Economic Community of West African States and the African Union. It also called on universities, research institutions and policy organisations to intensify research and sustained dialogue on terrorism, religious freedom, human security, international law and national sovereignty. The roundtable was chaired by the Director of CEPAD, Rev. Fr. Dr Innocent T. Jooji, who also presented a paper on counter-terrorism in Nigeria and the question of US military intervention. Jooji highlighted concerns about national sovereignty, weak oversight, external dependency, human rights and the potential use of foreign military involvement as propaganda by insurgent groups. He recommended recalibrating Nigeria’s security partnership with the United States by strengthening domestic security capacity, improving parliamentary oversight, expanding deradicalisation and development programmes, and enhancing regional cooperation. The event also featured two thematic roundtable sessions examining religious freedom, security and defence, as well as international relations and law. The communiqué was signed by Jooji; the Programme Manager of Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, Nigeria, Comrade Angela Odah; and Dr Ikechukwu Maxwell Ukandu of the conference secretariat. Background: Nigeria has sustained military operations against Boko Haram and ISWAP, particularly in the North-East, while insecurity involving armed groups, banditry, kidnappings and other forms of violence has continued to challenge security agencies. The debate over US involvement has also drawn attention to the balance between international security assistance, Nigeria’s sovereignty and civilian protection. The Responsibility to Protect (R2P), endorsed by United Nations member states in 2005, places responsibility on states to protect their populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, while providing for international assistance and collective action through established UN mechanisms.
